deep.topic: Week 4 of Elementary Mathematics II treated conceptually: what the objects in a limit statement actually are and why each continuity criterion is there. Covers the three-condition definition of continuity at a point c (f(c) defined, lim as x approaches c exists, and the two are equal), one-sided limits and the existence criterion that the left and right limits must agree on one finite real number, what an open circle and a shaded dot each encode on a graph, and why 'limit equals infinity' is a description of failure rather than a value. Covers the four types of discontinuity (removable, jump, infinite, essential) as names for which criterion fails and in what way, including why a removable one can be repaired by redefining a single point and a jump or infinite one cannot. No computation is required; every question asks what breaks without a given condition.

fast.topic: Week 4 traces Nigeria's constitutional development from Lord Lugard's advisory Nigerian Council of 1914 (36 members, six unofficial) through four constitutions. Sir Hugh Clifford, who took over in 1919, produced Nigeria's first written constitution in 1922: three units (Lagos Colony, Southern Provinces, Northern Provinces), a 45-member legislative council of 26 official Europeans, 15 nominated members and 4 elected Nigerians (3 Lagos, 1 Calabar), the elective principle, and Cameroon joining Nigeria, but with the Governor's veto, no local input and no Northern representation. Interim governors are Sir Graham Thompson (1926), Sir Donald Cameron (1930-1936, who abolished the Lieutenant Governor's office and the provincial court and introduced separation of powers) and Bernard Bourdillon (1935). Sir Arthur Richards' constitution of 1947-1951 introduced regionalism, three regional Houses of Assembly, a bicameral North, 28 Nigerians of 45 council members with 4 elected, and two Nigerians on the Executive Council in 1949. Macpherson, Governor from 1948, consulted widely and in 1951 created the 136-member House of Representatives and the Council of Ministers with the Governor as Prime Minister and twelve ministers, but it fell within three years to Enahoro's motion for independence; Sir Oliver Lyttleton, a Colonial Secretary rather than a Governor, then introduced federalism in 1954, regional Premiers, a regionalised judiciary, Lagos as Federal Capital Territory and revenue allocation by derivation. The second strand covers the parties: Herbert Macaulay's NNDP (1923, Lagos Daily News, winning all three Lagos seats in 1923, 1928 and 1933), the Nigeria Youth Movement (1935, Ernest Ikoli and Samuel Akisanya, the Daily Service, taking all elective seats from the NNDP in 1938 and destroyed by internal disputes in 1944), the NCNC (August 1944, Macaulay as first President and Nnamdi Azikiwe as first General Secretary, the West African Pilot, the protest delegation against the 1946 constitution), the Action Group (Ibadan, 1951, from Egbe Omo Oduduwa of 1945 founded by Awolowo, the Ooni and Ajasin), and the NPC (1951, from Jam'iyyar Mutanen Arewa, founded by Ahmadu Bello the Sardauna of Sokoto, Tafawa Balewa, Yahaya Gusau and Aminu Kano), plus the four criticisms of Nigerian parties: ethnocentrism, lack of ideology, a weakened centre and ethnic interest over national interest. The third strand is the weekly summary on the Amalgamation of 1914 that united Northern and Southern Nigeria, its two schools of thought (that it merely formalised pre-existing inter-group relations, or that it created a deeply divided nation) and the views of Dudley, Olusanya, E. Osaghae, Claude Ake and Lord Lugard on the civil war, national integration, and the failure of post-independence leaders to address colonial legacies.

deep.topic: Conceptual hour on Week 4 of General Physics II: what the quantities in DC circuit analysis and electrostatic dipoles actually are, and why each rule holds. Covers ideal versus real voltage and current sources, the meaning of internal resistance and the emf/terminal-voltage distinction, why a zeroed voltage source becomes a short and a zeroed current source an open circuit, the linearity that superposition and the Thevenin and Norton theorems depend on, and why a reference node may be set to zero in nodal analysis. Also covers the electric dipole moment as a vector from minus q to plus q, why the dipole potential falls as one over r squared and vanishes on the equatorial plane, why the axial and equatorial fields differ in size and direction, and why a dipole feels torque but no net force in a uniform field. Finally, why polarisation of a dielectric lowers the field and raises the capacitance. No numerical work is required in this session.

fast.topic: The fast hour covers styling HTML elements with CSS, starting from the idea that CSS separates content (HTML) from presentation. It defines selectors as patterns that target elements and walks through the five named types: type selectors (p), class selectors (.button), ID selectors (#header), the universal selector (*), and descendant selectors (article p), then shows selectors and properties combined as div.container .feature. It groups properties into colour (color, background-color, border-color), typography (font-family, font-size, font-weight), layout (width, height, margin, padding, display), positioning (position with top, right, bottom, left) and background (background-image, background-repeat, background-size). The CSS Box Model is analysed as content, padding, border and margin, with the worked total: a div of width 200px and height 100px with 20px padding, 2px border and 10px margin occupies 264px by 164px. Layout is covered through display (block, inline, inline-block), the float property, Flexbox and the two-dimensional CSS Grid with grid-template-columns and gap. Text styling covers font-family fallback lists, font-size units (px, em, %), font-weight, color, text-decoration, text-align, line-height, letter-spacing, text-shadow and text-transform, plus responsive typography via fluid vw sizing, media queries such as max-width 768px, and relative em and rem units. The Flexbox block defines flex container, flex item, main axis and cross axis, then covers display: flex and inline-flex, flex-direction (row, row-reverse, column, column-reverse), justify-content (flex-start, flex-end, center, space-between, space-around, space-evenly), align-items and align-self (flex-start, flex-end, center, baseline, stretch), the flex-grow, flex-shrink and flex-basis properties and their flex shorthand order, nested flex containers, and flex-wrap (nowrap, wrap, wrap-reverse). It closes with best practices: meaningful class and ID names, grouping related properties, prioritising external CSS files and cross-browser testing.

deep.topic: Week 4 Algorithm Concepts taken conceptually: what an algorithm is as distinct from a computer program, why the five-step development process puts a high-level algorithm before stepwise refinement, and why representation must supply sequence, selection and repetition. Then the analysis side: what priori analysis can settle before any code exists and what only posterior analysis can report, what Big O actually measures and what it deliberately throws away, and why worst case rather than best case is the figure normally quoted. Finally the characteristics and design considerations as claims about cost and failure: what language independence buys, what robustness means beyond correctness, and why a better algorithm rather than more hardware is what delivers scalability in the e-commerce case study.

fast.topic: This week covers paragraph construction and punctuation. The paragraph deck defines a paragraph as an individual unit of thought within a written composition and names the four components of a good paragraph: unity (a single central theme with no digression), coherence (ideas ordered logically and joined by cohesive links such as conjunctions and pronouns), the topic sentence, and one idea at a time. It distinguishes the topic sentence, which states the main idea and usually opens the paragraph, from supporting sentences or supporting details, using the Body Positivity specimen, and states the rule that five paragraphs require five topic sentences. It then sorts transition words into categories: addition, contrast, comparison, cause and effect, emphasis, sequence or order, illustration or example, conclusion or summary, time, and clarification. The punctuation deck sets out four uses of punctuation, namely changing the meaning, emphasising a point, conveying nuance, and clarifying ambiguity, illustrated by Let's eat, Grandma and I like cooking, my family, and pets. It then covers the period, comma, semicolon, colon, apostrophe, quotation marks, question mark, exclamation point, hyphen, dash with the em dash and en dash distinguished, ellipsis, parentheses, brackets, slash, and ampersand, each with its rule and examples. The week's summary strand adds writing strategies treated as analogous to programming languages, listing persuasion, narration, description, exposition, comparison, contrast, cause and effect, problem-solution, definition, chronological order, and process analysis, plus tone and style, audience awareness, editing and revision, and the four sentence types declarative, interrogative, imperative, and exclamatory.

deep.topic: Week 4 of Elementary Mathematics II worked as problems: taking numbers off graphs and out of formulas. Covers reading lim as x approaches c from the left, from the right, the two-sided limit and the value f(c) from a described graph, and classifying the point as removable, jump or infinite from the pair of one-sided limits. Covers the algebraic cases the deck uses — lim(x→3) of 2x+1 read off a line of slope 2 and intercept 1, lim(x→1) of (x²−1)/(x−1) by factoring and cancelling, and one-sided limits of |x| and |x|/x at 0 — plus choosing a constant that makes a piecewise function continuous at its joining point. Also covers diagnosing wrong routes, in particular treating the indeterminate form 0/0 as proof that a limit does not exist, and checking a classification against the graph before quoting it.

fast.topic: This week's practical is the experimental verification of Kirchhoff's Current Law, the first of Kirchhoff's two circuit laws, which follows from conservation of electric charge and states that the sum of the currents entering a junction equals the sum of those leaving it. The circuit is built on a breadboard from five variable resistors, two DC power supplies and three ammeters: R1 to R5 are set to 10, 1, 2.5, 7 and 5 kilohms, both supplies are put on the 50 V maximum-output range and their emfs dialled to 9 V. The three branch currents I1, I2 and I3 at the node are then recorded, and the run is repeated with the emf raised in regular 3 V steps to 12 V and 15 V. Verification is done by computing I3 as I1 plus I2 for each row, keeping the sign convention that currents entering the node are positive and those leaving are negative, and comparing that computed value with the current the third ammeter actually measured. The measured I2 is negative throughout, which simply means that branch carries current away from the junction, and in every row the algebraic sum reproduces the measured I3 exactly. The conclusion is that no charge accumulates at the junction and that KCL holds independently of the emf applied, so the node equation minus I1 minus I2 plus I3 equals zero is confirmed by experiment.

deep.topic: Problem-solving hour on the same Week 4 material of General Physics II. Sets up and executes numerical work on real sources (finding current and terminal voltage from emf, internal resistance and load, with the power balance as a check), on multi-source resistive networks by superposition, by nodal analysis with a chosen reference node, and by reduction to a Thevenin or Norton equivalent. Then on electric dipoles: computing the dipole moment from charge and separation, the far-field potential k p cos theta over r squared, the axial and equatorial field magnitudes and directions, and the torque and potential energy of a dipole in a uniform field. Finally a parallel-plate capacitor problem with a dielectric inserted at fixed charge. Emphasis throughout is on choosing the right relation, carrying units, and diagnosing the specific wrong routes that give plausible but incorrect numbers.

fast.topic: Week 4 review: re-work every check question you got wrong Mon-Thu, then cold, on paper, classify one discontinuity of each of the four types off a described graph, solve one DC network twice - once by nodal analysis and once by Thevenin - and confirm the two agree, and apply the Big O loop rules to one nested and one sequential loop. Finish by settling which two topics Sunday gets.

deep.topic: Week 4 Algorithm Concepts taken as practice: tracing the lecture's own algorithms by hand and writing them out. You trace the sum-and-count flowchart to a printed value and a decision count, work the maximum-of-a-set problem through the five development steps, and write the refined pseudocode using sequence, selection and repetition correctly. You then apply the Big O loop rules to concrete code fragments — a decrementing loop, a halving loop, nested loops — and diagnose faulty or wasteful solutions: a maximum initialised to zero, selection used where repetition was needed, and an O(n squared) pairwise comparison where one pass would do.

checks.topic: Week 4 of Elementary Mathematics II treated conceptually: what the objects in a limit statement actually are and why each continuity criterion is there. Covers the three-condition definition of continuity at a point c (f(c) defined, lim as x approaches c exists, and the two are equal), one-sided limits and the existence criterion that the left and right limits must agree on one finite real number, what an open circle and a shaded dot each encode on a graph, and why 'limit equals infinity' is a description of failure rather than a value. Covers the four types of discontinuity (removable, jump, infinite, essential) as names for which criterion fails and in what way, including why a removable one can be repaired by redefining a single point and a jump or infinite one cannot. No computation is required; every question asks what breaks without a given condition.

questions.q: The definition of continuity at c lists 'f(c) is defined' as a separate condition, even though the third condition already says lim(x→c) f(x) = f(c). Why is the first condition not redundant?
options: Because a limit can exist without being finite, and only a finite limit can be compared with a function value in the first place
Because if f(c) were undefined then the two one-sided limits would automatically disagree with each other at c
Because the equation lim(x→c) f(x) = f(c) asserts nothing if its right-hand side names no number; the condition guarantees there is something to compare the limit with
Because f(c) has to be computed before the limit can be computed, so the conditions must be checked in the stated order
questions.concept: Why 'f(c) is defined' is an independent condition — an equation between a number and an undefined symbol is not false, it is meaningless.
questions.why: Condition (iii) is an equality between two numbers. If f(c) does not exist there is no right-hand side, so the equality cannot be tested at all; condition (i) exists to supply it. The limit and the value are computed independently, so no ordering or automatic consequence is involved.

questions.q: A curve rises without bound on both sides of x = 2, so lim(x→2⁻) f(x) = +∞ and lim(x→2⁺) f(x) = +∞. The two one-sided results are written the same, yet we still say lim(x→2) f(x) does not exist. Why?
options: Because a limit must be one finite real number that the values settle on, and +∞ records unbounded growth instead of any such number
Because f is undefined at x = 2, and a limit cannot exist at a point where the function has no value
Because agreement of the one-sided limits only counts towards existence when the function is already continuous at the point
Because the +∞ reached from the left is a different object from the +∞ reached from the right, so the two do not genuinely agree
questions.concept: What 'the limit exists' asserts: a single finite real number, not merely matching one-sided descriptions.
questions.why: Existence of a limit means the function values approach one real number arbitrarily closely. The symbol +∞ is not a real number; it is shorthand for the values escaping every bound, so the limit fails to exist however the two sides are written.

questions.q: Why is a removable discontinuity called removable?
options: Because the hole is a single point of zero width, so it does not disturb the overall shape of the graph
Because deleting the point c from the domain of f leaves a function with no discontinuity anywhere in its domain
Because factoring the expression and cancelling the common factor algebraically makes the discontinuity go away
Because lim(x→c) f(x) already exists as one finite value L, so setting f(c) := L makes all three continuity conditions hold at that point
questions.concept: Removability is a statement about the limit already existing — the repair is redefining one function value, not editing the formula or the domain.
questions.why: The limit supplies exactly the number the missing or misplaced value should have been, so a single redefinition satisfies conditions (i), (ii) and (iii) simultaneously. Cancelling a factor produces a different function, and deleting the point removes the question rather than repairing the function.

questions.q: At a jump discontinuity at x = a, why can no choice of the value f(a) make f continuous at a?
options: Because f grows without bound on at least one side of a, so no finite value assigned at a could ever match the behaviour of the curve there
Because continuity first requires lim(x→a) f(x) to exist, and that limit is decided by the two branches alone, which a value assigned at the single point a cannot alter
Because the two branches meet a with different slopes, and continuity at a point requires the slopes on the two sides to match there
Because at a jump the value f(a) is always undefined, and an undefined quantity cannot be given a new value by redefinition
questions.concept: The limit is built only from x ≠ a, so redefining f(a) can fix condition (iii) but never condition (ii).
questions.why: Condition (ii) fails at a jump because L⁻ ≠ L⁺, and both of those are computed from values of f at points other than a. Changing f(a) changes only the value being compared, never the disagreement between the sides.

questions.q: On a graph at x = 1 both branches of the curve run into an open circle at (1, 4), and a shaded dot is plotted at (1, −2). What do the two symbols encode?
options: The open circle records the height both branches approach, so lim(x→1) f(x) = 4, while the shaded dot records the value, so f(1) = −2
The open circle records the value, so f(1) = 4, and the shaded dot marks a further point the curve happens to pass through
Both symbols record outputs of f at x = 1, so f takes the two values 4 and −2 there
The open circle shows f is undefined at x = 1, so f(1) does not exist and the shaded dot carries no information
questions.concept: A graph records the limit and the value as two separate pieces of information, drawn with two different symbols.
questions.why: An open circle marks a height the curve approaches but does not attain, which is the limit; a shaded dot is the one point where the function actually takes a value. Here the limit exists and equals 4 while f(1) = −2, a removable discontinuity.

questions.q: A graph is an unbroken curve everywhere except that at x = c the pen must be lifted for one isolated point and then put down again immediately, the curve continuing at the same height. Which continuity condition has failed at c?
options: Condition (ii): the limit fails to exist, since the pen left the curve at c and a limit cannot survive a lift
No condition fails, because one isolated point has no width and so cannot affect whether f is continuous at c
Conditions (ii) and (iii) both fail, since a lifted pen means the left and right approaches have arrived at different heights
Condition (i) or condition (iii): the limit exists, but f(c) is either undefined or plotted at a different height from the limit
questions.concept: Translating the pen-lifting picture into which of the three algebraic conditions has failed.
questions.why: The curve continuing at the same height on both sides means L⁻ = L⁺, so the limit exists and condition (ii) holds. The lift therefore records the single point being missing (condition (i)) or sitting at the wrong height (condition (iii)) — the removable case.

questions.q: How does an essential discontinuity differ from an infinite discontinuity?
options: An essential discontinuity happens at a point outside the domain of f, whereas an infinite discontinuity happens at a point that is inside the domain
An essential discontinuity has one one-sided limit finite and the other infinite, whereas an infinite discontinuity has both one-sided limits infinite

At an infinite discontinuity each one-sided limit fails in a definite direction, ±∞, giving a vertical asymptote; at an essential discontinuity a one-sided limit settles on nothing at all, finite or infinite
An essential discontinuity is by definition one that cannot be removed, whereas an infinite discontinuity can be removed by giving f a value at the asymptote
questions.concept: The four types classify how a one-sided limit fails; infinite is an organised failure with a direction, essential is failure to settle at all.
questions.why: An infinite discontinuity still describes the behaviour precisely — the values run off to +∞ or −∞ and the graph hugs a vertical line. An essential discontinuity is the case where even that description is unavailable because the values keep oscillating without approaching anything.

questions.q: A student verifies that lim(x→c⁻) f(x) = lim(x→c⁺) f(x) and concludes that f is continuous at c. What has actually been established, and what has not?
options: Nothing has been established, because one-sided limits carry no information about the two-sided limit at c
The limit at c exists, but continuity further requires f(c) to be defined and to equal that limit, and comparing the two sides tests neither
Continuity has been established, because equality of the one-sided limits is precisely what continuity at a point means
The limit exists and f(c) must equal it, because a curve necessarily passes through the height it approaches
questions.concept: Equality of one-sided limits is the existence criterion for the limit, which is only condition (ii) of three.
questions.why: Matching one-sided limits establishes that lim(x→c) f(x) exists. Whether f(c) exists, and whether it equals that limit, is independent information — the removable case is exactly where the sides agree and the value does not.

questions.q: Explain why a removable discontinuity can be repaired by changing the function at exactly one point, while a jump discontinuity cannot be repaired by changing the function at any number of single points.
questions.concept: Which continuity condition each type of discontinuity breaks, and the fact that the limit is computed from x ≠ c only.
questions.why: A full answer says: the limit at c is determined entirely by values of f at points other than c, so redefining f(c) can never change lim(x→c) f(x). At a removable discontinuity the limit already exists and equals a single finite L, so conditions (ii) is already satisfied and only (i) or (iii) is broken; setting f(c) := L repairs exactly the broken condition. At a jump, the broken condition is (ii) itself — L⁻ ≠ L⁺ — and that inequality is a fact about the two branches, untouched by any value assigned at c. Repairing a jump would require moving a whole branch, which is a different function, not a repair.

questions.q: Explain why writing lim(x→3⁺) f(x) = +∞ should be read as a description of how the limit fails rather than as a value of the limit, and what would go wrong if we treated +∞ as an ordinary answer.
questions.concept: The meaning of limit existence — approach to a single finite real number — and why ∞ is a behaviour label, not a number.
questions.why: A full answer says: the limit exists means the values of f get and stay arbitrarily close to one fixed real number L. The notation +∞ says the opposite — the values eventually exceed every bound, so there is no L they settle near. It is retained because it records the direction of the failure, which distinguishes an infinite discontinuity from an essential one and tells us to draw a vertical asymptote. If +∞ were treated as an ordinary value we would have to accept it into arithmetic and into the continuity test lim = f(c), where f(c) must be a real number; we would also wrongly declare the two-sided limit to exist whenever both sides ran to +∞.

questions.q: Explain why the graphical test 'you can draw the graph through the point without lifting your pen' is equivalent to the three-condition definition of continuity, saying which kind of lift corresponds to which failed condition.
questions.concept: Mapping the visual criterion onto the algebraic one — the graph is a record of both the limit and the value.
questions.why: A full answer says: drawing without lifting requires that the ink arriving from the left, the ink arriving from the right and the plotted point at c all be at the same place. Ink arriving from the left is L⁻, ink from the right is L⁺, and the plotted point is f(c). A gap where no point is plotted is condition (i) failing; a break where the two branches arrive at different heights, or run off a vertical asymptote, is condition (ii) failing; a lone dot sitting off the curve while the branches agree is condition (iii) failing. Since these are the only three ways the pen can lift, the visual test and the definition agree exactly. It should also note that a sharp corner such as |x| at 0 involves no lift and so is not a discontinuity.

questions.q: Explain why the value f(c) plays no part in computing lim(x→c) f(x), and why the definition of continuity therefore has to state the equality of limit and value as a separate condition rather than deriving it.
questions.concept: The limit depends only on the punctured neighbourhood of c; continuity is the extra assertion that the function honours that approach at c itself.
questions.why: A full answer says: the limit describes what f does as x approaches c through values different from c, so the definition deliberately excludes x = c; this is what makes limits useful for expressions like (x²−1)/(x−1) that are undefined at the point. Consequently two functions agreeing everywhere except at c have identical limits there but can have different values at c, so no computation of the limit could ever reveal f(c). Continuity is precisely the extra claim that the function does not do something different at c from what its neighbours predict, and since that claim is not a consequence of the limit it must be imposed as its own condition.
