Covers ideal versus real voltage and current sources, the meaning of internal resistance and the emf/terminal-voltage distinction, why a zeroed voltage source becomes a short and a zeroed current source an open circuit, the linearity that superposition and the Thevenin and Norton theorems depend on, and why a reference node may be set to zero in nodal analysis. Also covers the electric dipole moment as a vector from minus q to plus q, why the dipole potential falls as one over r squared and vanishes on the equatorial plane, why the axial and equatorial fields differ in size and direction, and why a dipole feels torque but no net force in a uniform field. Finally, why polarisation of a dielectric lowers the field and raises the capacitance. No numerical work is required in this session.

questions.q: In a superposition analysis you must 'zero' each source in turn. What justifies replacing a zeroed ideal voltage source by a wire and a zeroed ideal current source by a gap?
options: A zeroed voltage source holds 0 V across itself no matter what current passes, which is exactly what a wire does; a zeroed current source passes 0 A no matter what voltage appears, which is exactly what a gap does.
A dead battery has no charge left, so nothing can pass through it, whereas a dead current source still conducts freely.
Both should really be replaced by open circuits; the short-circuit rule for a voltage source is only a drawing convention that saves redrawing the diagram.
Each zeroed source is replaced by its internal resistance, which is infinite for a voltage source and zero for a current source.
questions.concept: What 'zeroing' a source means physically: it is the element's defining constraint with the source strength set to zero, not the removal of the element.
questions.why: An ideal source is defined by the constraint it imposes. Setting the emf to zero leaves the constraint V = 0 across the element, which is a short. Setting the source current to zero leaves the constraint I = 0 through the element, which is an open circuit.

questions.q: A real cell's terminal voltage V is measured for several output currents I and the points fall on a straight line. What do the gradient and the vertical intercept represent?
options: The gradient is +r and the intercept is the terminal voltage at the maximum current the cell can supply.
The gradient is minus r and the vertical intercept is the emf.
The gradient is minus one over r and the vertical intercept is the emf.
The gradient is the emf and the vertical intercept is the internal resistance r.
questions.concept: Reading V = emf minus I r as the equation of a straight line, and using unit analysis to fix which combination of gradient gives a resistance.
questions.why: V = emf minus I r is y = c + m x with c = emf and m = minus r, so r is minus the gradient. Units confirm it: a gradient of volts per ampere is already an ohm, whereas its reciprocal would be a siemens. (The lecture slide states r is 'the negative reciprocal of the slope', which is wrong.)

questions.q: A student finds the power dissipated in a resistor of a two-battery circuit by computing the power each battery would produce alone and adding them. Why does this give the wrong answer even though superposition is valid for this circuit?
options: Because superposition only holds when the two sources have equal emfs.
Because zeroing one source alters the resistances of the network, so the single-source resistor values are not the real ones.
Because power depends on the square of the current, and the square of a sum is not the sum of the squares.
Because power is only dissipated while both sources are actually connected, so the single-source figures describe no real situation at all.
questions.concept: Superposition applies to quantities linear in the source strengths; power is quadratic, so it does not superpose even in a fully linear network.
questions.why: Superposition follows from linearity, and currents and voltages are linear in the source strengths. P = I squared R is quadratic, so P of (I1 + I2) is not P of I1 plus P of I2: the cross term 2 I1 I2 R is missing.

questions.q: To find the Thevenin resistance of a linear black box you switch off every independent source inside it and measure the resistance at the terminals. Why is the resistance measured with the sources off the right one to put in the equivalent circuit?
options: Switching the sources off removes their driving action but leaves every resistance in place, and linearity lets the source-driven and externally-driven responses add independently.
Switching them off is only a convenient approximation; strictly R_Th should be measured with the sources live, but the error is usually small.
The sources contain no resistance of their own, so whether they are on or off cannot change anything inside the box.
R_Th is a property of the load rather than of the box, so the internal state of the box is irrelevant.
questions.concept: Why R_Th is defined with the sources dead: linear superposition separates the box's response into a source term (V_Th) and a resistive term (R_Th) driven by the external world.
questions.why: For a linear box the terminal relation is V = V_Th minus I R_Th. V_Th is the part driven by the internal sources with no external current; R_Th is the part driven by an external test current with the internal sources dead. Superposition guarantees these two contributions add without interfering.

questions.q: In nodal analysis one node is chosen and simply declared to be at zero volts. Why does that not change any of the answers?
options: Because the chosen node is the one node that carries no current, so its potential cannot matter.
Because KCL requires the algebraic sum of all node voltages in a circuit to be zero anyway.
Because the negative terminal of a battery is genuinely at zero potential, so the choice is not really arbitrary at all.
Because only potential differences drive currents; adding the same constant to every node potential leaves every branch current unchanged.
questions.concept: Potential is defined only up to an additive constant; circuit behaviour depends on differences, so the reference node is a free gauge choice.
questions.why: Every branch current is (V at one end minus V at the other) divided by R. Shifting all node potentials by the same constant leaves each difference, and so each current, untouched. The reference node is a labelling convenience, not a physical fact.

questions.q: A permanent electric dipole sits in a perfectly uniform external field, tilted at 40 degrees to the field direction. What does it experience?
options: A net force pulling it toward the region of stronger field, but no torque.
Neither a net force nor a torque, since the two forces on it are equal and opposite.
Zero net force but a non-zero torque, because the equal and opposite forces act at two different points.
A net force along the field, together with a torque taken about the positive charge only.
questions.concept: The distinction between the resultant force (sum of forces, zero for equal and opposite forces) and the torque (which depends on where those forces act).
questions.why: The forces qE and minus qE are equal and opposite, so the vector sum is zero and the dipole does not accelerate. They act at points separated by d, so they form a couple of magnitude pE sin 40 degrees, which rotates the dipole toward alignment. A uniform field has no gradient, so there is nothing to pull it sideways.

questions.q: Why is the electric field at a point on the equatorial plane of a dipole directed antiparallel to the dipole moment p?
options: Because the negative charge is always the nearer of the two charges to any point on that plane.
Because the potential is zero everywhere on that plane, and the field must point from higher to lower potential along it.
Because in physics the dipole moment is defined to run from the positive charge to the negative charge.
Because both charges are equidistant from the point, so the components perpendicular to the axis cancel and the surviving components both point from +q toward minus q.
questions.concept: Vector superposition of the two Coulomb fields on the perpendicular bisector, and the fact that zero potential on a surface does not fix the field direction.
questions.why: On the bisector the two fields have equal magnitude. Resolve each into a component along the axis and one perpendicular to it: the perpendicular components are opposite and cancel, while the axial components both point from the positive charge toward the negative one, i.e. antiparallel to p.

questions.q: A charged, isolated parallel-plate capacitor has a dielectric slab slid between its plates. Why does the field between the plates fall and the capacitance rise?
options: The slab conducts a little charge from one plate across to the other, so the stored charge and hence the field are reduced.
The applied field polarises the slab, producing bound surface charges whose own field opposes the plate field, so E and hence V fall while Q is fixed, and C = Q/V rises.
The slab effectively increases the plate separation, and capacitance grows in proportion to separation.
The slab raises the permittivity of free space itself, so the constant epsilon-nought takes a larger value inside the gap.
questions.concept: Dielectric polarisation as bound (not free) charge that partially cancels the applied field; and C = Q/V as the definition that then forces C upward.
questions.why: A dielectric is an insulator, so no free charge crosses it. Molecular charge shifts a little, leaving bound sheets of positive and negative charge on the slab faces whose field opposes the plate field. E drops by the factor kappa, V = Ed drops with it, and since Q is unchanged C = Q/V rises by kappa.

questions.q: Explain why an ideal current source must have infinite internal resistance while an ideal voltage source must have zero internal resistance.
questions.concept: Source models: internal resistance as the mechanism by which load conditions feed back on what the source delivers.
questions.why: A full answer models a real voltage source as an emf in series with r, so V = emf minus I r: any r greater than zero makes the delivered voltage depend on the load current, and only r = 0 makes it independent, which is the definition of ideal. It models a real current source as an ideal current source in parallel with r, so the load steals a share I_r = V/r of the source current: only r infinite makes that share zero at any load voltage, so the delivered current is load-independent. The two conditions are the same requirement — that the internal element carry no information about the load — applied to the two complementary constraints.

questions.q: Explain why both superposition and Thevenin's theorem fail if the black box contains a non-linear element such as a diode.
questions.concept: Linearity as the precondition for both theorems, and what specifically breaks when it is absent.
questions.why: A full answer says that both theorems rest on the terminal response being a linear function of the source strengths, so that responses to separate causes add. A diode's current is an exponential function of its voltage, so doubling a source does not double the current and two sources acting together do not produce the sum of their separate effects — superposition's premise is simply false. Thevenin's theorem fails for the same reason: with a diode inside, the terminal relation V against I is a curve, not the straight line V = V_Th minus I R_Th, so no single emf-plus-resistor pair can reproduce the box's behaviour at more than one operating point.

questions.q: Explain why the potential of a dipole falls off as one over r squared while that of a single point charge falls off as one over r, and why the dipole potential is exactly zero everywhere on the equatorial plane.
questions.concept: Cancellation between the two charges' potentials, and how the residual depends on the small path difference to the two charges.
questions.why: A full answer computes V as kq/r_plus minus kq/r_minus. Because the total charge is zero, the leading one-over-r terms cancel exactly and what remains is proportional to the difference in the two distances, which for r much greater than d is about d cos theta. That gives V = k q d cos theta / r squared = k p cos theta / r squared, one power of r faster than a point charge because the surviving term is a difference rather than a sum. On the equatorial plane every point is equidistant from +q and minus q, so the two potentials are equal and opposite and cancel completely, giving V = 0 there; equivalently cos 90 degrees = 0. It should add that this does not make E zero there, since E depends on how V changes across the plane, not on its value on it.

questions.q: Explain why a dipole experiences no net force in a uniform field, but is pulled toward the stronger-field region when the field is non-uniform.
questions.concept: Net force on a dipole as the difference between two nearly cancelling forces, i.e. a field gradient effect rather than a field effect.
questions.why: A full answer says the two forces are qE at the position of +q and minus qE at the position of minus q. If E is the same at both places the two forces are exactly equal and opposite and their sum is zero, leaving only the couple. If E varies in space, the charge sitting where the field is stronger feels the larger force, and the residual net force is q times the difference in E across the separation d, that is proportional to the gradient of E rather than to E itself. Once the dipole has aligned with the field, the positive charge sits in the stronger-field region, so the residual force pulls the dipole into the stronger field. It should note the net force can therefore be zero even in a non-uniform field if the dipole is oriented so that the field is the same at both charges.

checks.topic: Week 4 Algorithm Concepts taken conceptually: what an algorithm is as distinct from a computer program, why the five-step development process puts a high-level algorithm before stepwise refinement, and why representation must supply sequence, selection and repetition. Then the analysis side: what priori analysis can settle before any code exists and what only posterior analysis can report, what Big O actually measures and what it deliberately throws away, and why worst case rather than best case is the figure normally quoted. Finally the characteristics and design considerations as claims about cost and failure: what language independence buys, what robustness means beyond correctness, and why a better algorithm rather than more hardware is what delivers scalability in the e-commerce case study.

questions.q: The lecture insists that an algorithm should not be dependent on any programming language. What does that independence actually buy you?
options: The same plan can be converted into a program in whichever language the implementer chooses, so the design work survives a change of implementation language.
It guarantees the algorithm will take the same number of seconds to run on every machine.
It removes the need for the refinement step, because the detail that refinement adds is language-specific anyway.
It lowers the algorithm's Big O, because no language or compiler overhead is counted in the total.
questions.concept: Algorithm as a language-independent plan designed by people, which must then be converted into a program
questions.why: An algorithm is a plan for solving a problem; keeping it free of any one language is what lets the same plan be converted into a program in any language. It says nothing about seconds, does not remove refinement (which is driven by who implements it, their knowledge and the machine specification), and Big O is unaffected by language choice.

questions.q: Why does the development process require a high-level algorithm (Step 3) before refinement (Step 4), rather than writing the detailed version straight away?
options: Because focusing on every minor detail before you have at least a solution is time-wasting and costly, so the main parts of the solution are settled first.
Because only the high-level algorithm is reviewed in Step 5; the refined version is never reviewed.
Because refinement is optional and is only performed when the client complains about the result.
Because the client writes the high-level algorithm and the programmer writes the refinement.
questions.concept: Purpose of high-level algorithm development versus stepwise refinement
questions.why: The deck's stated reason is economic: detail is expensive to produce and expensive to throw away, so you commit to the main parts of the solution first and add detail once the shape is right. Review comes after refinement, refinement is not optional, and both steps are the programmer's work.

questions.q: What can posterior analysis tell you that priori analysis cannot?
options: Which of two candidate algorithms has the faster-growing running time as n increases.
The actual space and running time requirements of the algorithm once implemented in a particular programming language.
Whether the algorithm terminates for every possible input.
Whether the original problem description relied on unstated assumptions.
questions.concept: Priori (pre-implementation, language-independent) versus posterior (post-implementation, actual space and time) analysis
questions.why: Posterior analysis is carried out after implementation in a particular language and deals precisely with the space and running time requirements. Growth-rate comparison is exactly what priori analysis does without running anything, and the other two belong to Step 5 review and Step 1 description.

questions.q: Big O describes the growth rate of an algorithm. What does using it deliberately discard?
options: The number of times the innermost statement of a nested loop is executed.
Constant factors and machine speed, so two algorithms in the same class can still differ substantially in actual seconds.
The distinction between best, worst and average case, which Big O has no way of expressing.
The input size n, which Big O treats as a fixed quantity.
questions.concept: What Big O measures (growth with n) and what it abstracts away (constants, hardware, language)
questions.why: Big O is a statement about how the requirement grows with n, so constants and machine-specific speed drop out; that is why actual seconds need posterior analysis. Innermost-statement counts are how you derive the class, best/worst/average are each given their own Big O, and n is the variable, not a constant.

questions.q: Why is worst case time complexity normally the figure quoted for an algorithm, rather than best case?
options: Because the best case is mathematically impossible to determine for most algorithms.
Because the best case is always O(1) and therefore carries no information.
Because it is a guarantee: it bounds the maximum time for any input of size n, so a system sized on it cannot be caught out.
Because worst case and average case turn out to be identical for every algorithm.
questions.concept: Best, worst and average case as three different measures over inputs of the same size n
questions.why: Worst case is defined as the maximum time required for an input of size n, which makes it the only one of the three that is a guarantee. Best case is usually easy to determine, is not always constant, and average case (the typical input of size n) is a distinct measure.

questions.q: An algorithm produces the right output for every input it was designed for, but its behaviour on an empty input list was never defined at all — it simply was not considered. Which design consideration has been violated?
options: Modularity
Extensibility
Robustness
Simplicity
questions.concept: Robustness (the solution to the problem is clearly defined) as distinct from correctness, modularity and extensibility
questions.why: Robustness in this course means the solution to the problem is clearly defined; an undefined case is a gap in the definition, not a wrong answer. Modularity is about breaking the solution into smaller steps, extensibility about another designer updating it later, simplicity about being easy to understand.

questions.q: Why must an algorithm's representation contain sequence, selection and repetition?
options: Because a flowchart offers exactly three symbol shapes, and each form maps onto one of them.
Because these three are simply the components of an algorithm — its input, its process and its output — appearing here under different names.
Because Big O analysis can only be applied to algorithms built from these three control structures.
Because every programming language provides them, which is what makes the algorithm easily translatable into any of them.
questions.concept: Sequence, selection and repetition as the representation forms that make algorithms translatable into programming languages
questions.why: The stated reason is translatability: representing the algorithm in forms every language supplies means it can be carried into any of them. Flowcharts use more than three symbols, the components of an algorithm are input/process/output (a separate list), and Big O applies regardless of control structure.

questions.q: In the case study, an e-commerce platform serving millions of users fixed its recommendation problem by adopting a well-designed algorithm (collaborative filtering) rather than by buying more servers. Conceptually, why does the algorithm change help where hardware would not?
options: Because collaborative filtering runs in O(1) time regardless of how many users there are.
Because hardware can only affect the space an algorithm needs, never the time it takes.
Because posterior analysis showed the bottleneck was disk capacity rather than computation.
Because a better algorithm changes how the work grows with the number of users, while more hardware only improves the constant factor.
questions.concept: Scalability as a property of growth rate, which is why algorithm design rather than hardware determines it
questions.why: Hardware multiplies throughput by a constant; the growth rate is untouched, so a badly-growing solution simply fails a little later. Changing the algorithm changes the growth rate itself, which is what the course means by scalability. Collaborative filtering is not constant-time, hardware certainly affects time, and the case study reports a recommendation-quality and scale problem, not a disk one.

questions.q: Explain why priori analysis can rank two algorithms against each other even though it never runs either of them, and why that ranking is still trusted.
questions.concept: Priori analysis and growth rate as machine-independent properties of the algorithm itself
questions.why: A full answer says that priori analysis is carried out before implementation in any particular programming language and works on the structure of the algorithm itself — how many times each statement is executed as a function of the input size n — not on any measured time. Because that count is a property of the plan rather than of the machine, compiler or language, it does not change when any of those change; Big O then expresses it as a growth rate. The ranking is trusted because growth rate is the factor that dominates as n increases: whatever the constants, the faster-growing algorithm eventually loses and keeps losing. What priori analysis cannot give is the actual seconds or bytes on a given machine, which is the job of posterior analysis after implementation.

questions.q: Explain why a loop whose variable is divided by a constant amount each pass is O(log n) while a loop whose variable is decremented by a constant amount is O(n) — in terms of what happens to the number of passes when n doubles.
questions.concept: Deriving the O(n) and O(log n) loop rules from what the loop variable does per pass
questions.why: A full answer reasons from the number of passes. If the loop variable falls by a constant amount, reaching the stopping point takes a number of passes proportional to n, so doubling n doubles the passes: that is linear, O(n). If the loop variable is divided by a constant each pass, each pass removes a fixed fraction of what is left, so the passes count how many times n can be divided before hitting the limit; doubling n adds just one extra pass. A cost that grows by a fixed additive amount when n doubles is logarithmic, hence O(log n). The mechanism to state is 'constant amount removed per pass' versus 'constant factor removed per pass' — not that one loop merely looks shorter.

questions.q: Explain why most algorithm failures can be traced back to Step 1, problem description, rather than to the writing of the steps themselves.
questions.concept: Problem description issues — unstated assumptions, ambiguity, incompleteness — and the client/programmer gap that produces them
questions.why: A full answer identifies the structural cause: two different parties are involved — the client, who wants a solution, and the programmer, who provides it — and they do not share the same background knowledge. From that gap come the three listed issues: descriptions that rely on unstated assumptions, ambiguous descriptions and incomplete descriptions. The mechanism is that every later step inherits the description: problem analysis fixes the starting and ending points from it, the high-level algorithm encodes it, and refinement adds detail to it. An error there is not detected by any of those steps, because each is faithfully elaborating the wrong problem; the algorithm can be perfectly correct against the description and still be useless. That is why Step 5 review asks whether the algorithm actually solves the problem, and why the description issues are worth naming explicitly.

questions.q: Explain why writing the same step out on many separate lines is not a sustainable substitute for repetition — say precisely what breaks as the problem scales.
questions.concept: Repetition as a representation form, and why the algorithm must be independent of a particular input size
questions.why: A full answer explains that copying the step fixes the number of executions at write time, so the algorithm is bound to one particular input size; if the data grows, the algorithm itself must be rewritten, which contradicts the requirement that an algorithm should have a limited and countable number of instructions that nonetheless handles the general problem. It also multiplies the maintenance cost: a change to the step must be made in every copy, and each copy is a chance to introduce an inconsistency, which works against maintainability and correctness. Repetition instead binds the number of executions to a condition evaluated at run time, so one written step covers any input size, and the count of instructions stays finite regardless of n.

checks.topic: Week 4 of Elementary Mathematics II worked as problems: taking numbers off graphs and out of formulas. Covers reading lim as x approaches c from the left, from the right, the two-sided limit and the value f(c) from a described graph, and classifying the point as removable, jump or infinite from the pair of one-sided limits. Covers the algebraic cases the deck uses — lim(x→3) of 2x+1 read off a line of slope 2 and intercept 1, lim(x→1) of (x²−1)/(x−1) by factoring and cancelling, and one-sided limits of |x| and |x|/x at 0 — plus choosing a constant that makes a piecewise function continuous at its joining point. Also covers diagnosing wrong routes, in particular treating the indeterminate form 0/0 as proof that a limit does not exist, and checking a classification against the graph before quoting it.

questions.q: A graph shows: for x < 2 the curve rises and ends in an open circle at (2, 3); for x > 2 the curve begins at an open circle at (2, −4) and falls; a shaded dot is plotted at (2, 1). What is lim(x→2) f(x)?
options: 3, because the left branch arrives at the point first and sets the value of the limit there
1, because f(2) = 1 is the only value actually attained at x = 2 and the limit must take it
−0.5, the average of the two heights 3 and −4 that the branches arrive at
It does not exist, because lim(x→2⁻) f(x) = 3 and lim(x→2⁺) f(x) = −4 are unequal
questions.concept: The existence criterion applied to a graph: a two-sided limit exists only if both one-sided readings give the same finite number.
questions.why: The two branches approach different finite heights, 3 and −4, so no single value is being approached and the limit is DNE. Neither branch takes priority, no averaging is defined, and the plotted value at x = 2 is irrelevant to the limit.

questions.q: For the same graph (left branch into an open circle at (2, 3), right branch from an open circle at (2, −4), shaded dot at (2, 1)), what kind of discontinuity is at x = 2?
options: Jump discontinuity, because both one-sided limits are finite and they differ from each other
Removable discontinuity, because the shaded dot at (2, 1) only needs moving to close the gap
Infinite discontinuity, because the function falls by 7 units in no distance at all across x = 2
No discontinuity, because f(2) = 1 is defined and a defined function value means the function is continuous there
questions.concept: Classification from the pair (L⁻, L⁺): finite and unequal is a jump, whatever f(c) happens to be.
questions.why: L⁻ = 3 and L⁺ = −4 are both finite real numbers and are unequal, which is exactly the jump case. Removable requires the two to agree, infinite requires at least one to be ±∞, and being defined at a point is only one of the three continuity conditions.

questions.q: Evaluate lim(x→1) (x² − 1)/(x − 1) and state f(1) for f(x) = (x² − 1)/(x − 1).
options: The limit is 0 and f(1) = 0, because both the numerator and the denominator vanish at x = 1
The limit is 2 and f(1) is undefined, so the graph is the line y = x + 1 carrying a hole at (1, 2)
The limit does not exist and f(1) = 1, because the denominator is zero at x = 1
The limit is 2 and f(1) = 2, because cancelling the factor gives x + 1, which is perfectly defined at x = 1
questions.concept: Cancelling a common factor changes the formula but not the domain — the limit is repaired, the value at the point is not.
questions.why: For every x ≠ 1, (x−1)(x+1)/(x−1) = x + 1, so the limit is 1 + 1 = 2. The cancellation is only valid for x ≠ 1, so the original f still has 0/0 at x = 1 and f(1) remains undefined: a removable discontinuity with a hole at (1, 2).

questions.q: You evaluate lim(x→3) (2x + 1) graphically by drawing the line of slope 2 and y-intercept 1, then approaching x = 3 from both sides. What do you read off, and why?
options: 1, the y-intercept, since that is the height at which the graph meets the vertical axis
2, the slope, since near x = 3 the function is changing at the rate of 2 units per unit
7, since the line is unbroken at x = 3 and both branches run into the height 2(3) + 1 = 7
Nothing; a limit cannot be read off a graph and must be obtained algebraically instead
questions.concept: Reading a limit off an unbroken graph — the height the curve runs into, not a parameter of the formula.
questions.why: Approaching from the left through x = 2.9, 2.99 gives heights 6.8, 6.98 and from the right through x = 3.1, 3.01 gives 7.2, 7.02, so both sides run into 7. The slope and intercept are used to draw the line, not to answer the limit.

questions.q: For h(x) = |x|/x, what are the readings at x = 0?
options: lim(x→0⁻) h(x) = −1 and lim(x→0⁺) h(x) = 1, so lim(x→0) h(x) does not exist: a jump discontinuity at 0
lim(x→0) h(x) = 0, because the numerator |x| approaches 0 as x approaches 0 from either side
lim(x→0) h(x) = 1, because |x| and x always have the same magnitude, so the quotient is 1 throughout
lim(x→0) h(x) is ±∞, because the denominator approaches 0, which always produces an infinite discontinuity
questions.concept: Splitting an absolute value into its two branches before taking one-sided limits, and not assuming a zero denominator means an asymptote.
questions.why: For x > 0, |x| = x so h(x) = 1; for x < 0, |x| = −x so h(x) = −1. The graph is two horizontal rays at heights 1 and −1 with a break at 0, so the one-sided limits are finite and unequal: a jump, not an asymptote.

questions.q: A graph has a vertical dashed line at x = 3: to its left the curve plunges downward hugging the line, to its right it climbs upward hugging the line, and no dot of any kind is plotted at x = 3. Which reading is correct?
options: lim(x→3) f(x) = ∞ and f(3) = ∞, since both branches run off the top and bottom of the page
lim(x→3) f(x) does not exist and f(3) is undefined; the point is an infinite discontinuity
lim(x→3) f(x) does not exist but f(3) = 0, the height at which the asymptote crosses the x-axis
The discontinuity is removable, since redefining f(3) at a finite height closes the gap between the branches
questions.concept: Reading an infinite discontinuity: unbounded one-sided behaviour plus no shaded dot means DNE and no function value.
questions.why: The one-sided limits are −∞ and +∞, neither a real number, so the limit does not exist; the absence of a shaded dot means no value is assigned at x = 3. Unbounded behaviour on both sides with a vertical asymptote is the infinite case.

questions.q: A student writes: 'Substituting x = 1 into (x² − 1)/(x − 1) gives 0/0, which is undefined, therefore lim(x→1) f(x) does not exist.' Which correction is right?
options: Substitute a nearby value such as x = 1.001, read off 2.001, and quote that as the exact value of the limit
The conclusion is right; the correct description is that f has an infinite discontinuity at x = 1
0/0 should be read as 1, since a quantity divided by itself is 1, so the limit is 1
0/0 is an indeterminate form, not a verdict — it instructs you to factor and cancel: (x−1)(x+1)/(x−1) = x + 1 for x ≠ 1, so the limit is 2
questions.concept: What the indeterminate form 0/0 licenses: further work, not a conclusion about existence.
questions.why: 0/0 means direct substitution has failed to decide anything, because the numerator and denominator both vanish at the same point — typically because they share the factor (x − 1). Cancelling that factor for x ≠ 1 gives x + 1, whose limit at 1 is 2, so the limit exists and the discontinuity is removable.

questions.q: Let f(x) = x² for x < 2 and f(x) = kx for x ≥ 2. Which value of k makes f continuous at x = 2, and on what grounds?
options: k = 4, so that the second branch kx delivers the value 4 that x² has at the joining point
k = 0, so that the second branch is flat at height 0 and therefore introduces no jump at x = 2
k = 2, because continuity needs lim(x→2⁻) f(x) = 4 to equal lim(x→2⁺) f(x) = 2k, which also equals f(2) = 2k
No value of k works, because x² and kx are different formulas and the graph must break where the formula changes
questions.concept: Setting up a continuity condition at a joining point: equate left limit, right limit and function value, then solve.
questions.why: The left limit is 2² = 4 and the right limit is k·2 = 2k, which is also f(2) since the second branch owns x = 2. Setting 4 = 2k gives k = 2; the common error k = 4 substitutes the value instead of solving for the coefficient.

questions.q: Explain why getting 0/0 when you substitute into a quotient does not entitle you to write 'limit DNE', and explain what the form is actually telling you about the numerator and denominator.
questions.concept: Indeterminate form as a signal to simplify, and why cancellation is legitimate inside a limit.
questions.why: A full answer says: 0/0 is indeterminate — quotients producing it can have any limit at all, or none, so the form by itself decides nothing. It tells you that the numerator and denominator both vanish at the point, which for polynomials means they share a factor of (x − c). Because a limit as x approaches c uses only values with x ≠ c, that factor is nonzero throughout the computation and may be cancelled; the simplified expression agrees with the original everywhere except at c and so has the same limit. It should end with the worked instance: (x−1)(x+1)/(x−1) = x + 1 for x ≠ 1, giving limit 2. It should also note that 0/0 combined with a shared factor is the signature of a removable discontinuity, unlike a nonzero-over-zero form, which signals an asymptote.

questions.q: Explain why testing continuity of a piecewise function at its joining point x = a requires three separate evaluations, and why confirming that the two formulas give the same number at x = a can still leave the function discontinuous there.
questions.concept: The three continuity conditions applied to a piecewise definition — the value at the joint is a separate declaration from the two branch formulas.
questions.why: A full answer says: the three quantities are lim(x→a⁻) f(x) from the branch valid below a, lim(x→a⁺) f(x) from the branch valid above a, and f(a) from whichever clause actually owns x = a. The first two must agree to give condition (ii), and the third must equal them for condition (iii). Substituting a into both formulas tests only the first pair, so if the definition assigns f(a) by a separate clause — for example f(x) = x² for x < 2, f(x) = 2x for x > 2, f(2) = 7 — the branch limits agree at 4 while f(2) = 7, leaving a removable discontinuity. It should also note that if no clause owns x = a then f(a) is undefined and condition (i) fails.

questions.q: On the graph with lim(x→2⁻) f(x) = 3, lim(x→2⁺) f(x) = −4 and a shaded dot at (2, 1), explain why the reading f(2) = 1 makes no difference to your answer for lim(x→2) f(x), and what it would take to change that answer.
questions.concept: The limit is computed from a punctured neighbourhood; only the branches can change it.
questions.why: A full answer says: the limit describes the heights the curve takes as x approaches 2 through values different from 2, so the isolated point at (2, 1) is never sampled and cannot enter the computation. The answer DNE comes from the disagreement 3 ≠ −4 between the two branches; moving the shaded dot to (2, 3), to (2, −4) or deleting it entirely leaves that disagreement intact and the limit still DNE. Only redrawing one of the branches so that both arrive at the same finite height would change the answer. It should note the corollary that f(2) matters for continuity — condition (iii) — but never for the limit itself.

questions.q: Explain why a graph with a vertical asymptote at x = 3 cannot be made continuous there by defining f(3) to be some very large number, and describe the check you would run on your classification before writing 'infinite discontinuity' as your answer.
questions.concept: Repair is only possible when the limit already exists; classifying by the one-sided limits rather than by the look of the picture.
questions.why: A full answer says: continuity at 3 needs lim(x→3) f(x) to exist first, and near an asymptote the values exceed every bound, so there is no finite L for f(3) to match. However large the assigned value, the curve passes it and keeps going, so condition (ii) still fails and condition (iii) has nothing to compare against — the repair argument that works for a hole is unavailable because the hole case has an existing limit and this one does not. The check is to read the two one-sided limits explicitly: if both are finite and equal it is removable, finite and unequal it is a jump, and only if at least one runs to +∞ or −∞ is it infinite; and to confirm that the values really do escape every bound rather than oscillating, which would make it essential instead.

checks.topic: Problem-solving hour on the same Week 4 material of General Physics II. Sets up and executes numerical work on real sources (finding current and terminal voltage from emf, internal resistance and load, with the power balance as a check), on multi-source resistive networks by superposition, by nodal analysis with a chosen reference node, and by reduction to a Thevenin or Norton equivalent. Then on electric dipoles: computing the dipole moment from charge and separation, the far-field potential k p cos theta over r squared, the axial and equatorial field magnitudes and directions, and the torque and potential energy of a dipole in a uniform field. Finally a parallel-plate capacitor problem with a dielectric inserted at fixed charge. Emphasis throughout is on choosing the right relation, carrying units, and diagnosing the specific wrong routes that give plausible but incorrect numbers.

questions.q: A cell of emf 12.0 V and internal resistance 0.50 ohm drives a 5.5 ohm load. What is the terminal voltage?
questions.concept: Using the total circuit resistance R + r to get the current before applying V = emf minus I r.
questions.why: I = 12.0/(5.5 + 0.50) = 2.00 A, so V = 12.0 minus (2.00)(0.50) = 11.0 V, which also equals I R = 2.00 times 5.5. The 10.9 V figure comes from using I = 12.0/5.5, i.e. forgetting r when finding the current; 13.0 V comes from adding I r instead of subtracting.

questions.q: A 12 V source through a 4 ohm resistor and a 6 V source through a 2 ohm resistor both feed node A, which returns to ground through a 4 ohm resistor. Using superposition, what current does the 12 V source ALONE drive through the 4 ohm ground resistor?
questions.concept: Executing one term of a superposition: short the other voltage source, reduce the network, then divide the resulting node voltage by the branch resistance.
questions.why: Short the 6 V source. The 12 V source then sees 4 ohm in series with (2 parallel 4) = 1.333 ohm, so I = 12/5.333 = 2.25 A and the node voltage is 2.25 times 1.333 = 3.00 V, giving 3.00/4 = 0.75 A in the ground resistor. 1.50 A is the total from both sources acting together, and 3.00 A is 12/4, which ignores the rest of the network.

questions.q: For that same network, the 4 ohm ground resistor is treated as the load and removed. The Thevenin equivalent seen at node A and ground is
options: 8.0 V in series with 1.33 ohm
6.0 V in series with 1.33 ohm
8.0 V in series with 6.0 ohm
9.0 V in series with 2.67 ohm
questions.concept: V_Th is the open-circuit voltage with the load removed, and R_Th is the source-free resistance at the terminals — a parallel combination here, not a series one.
questions.why: With the load removed the two branches are in series across 12 V and 6 V: (12 minus V)/4 = (V minus 6)/2 gives V_Th = 8.0 V. Shorting both sources leaves 4 parallel 2 = 1.33 ohm. Checking: 8.0/(1.33 + 4) = 1.50 A, the true load current. The 6.0 V option is the node voltage with the load still connected, and 6.0 ohm is 4 + 2 added in series by mistake.

questions.q: For the same network with the 4 ohm ground resistor in place, which KCL equation at node A is correct?
options: (V minus 12)/4 + (V minus 6)/2 = V/4
(12 minus V)/4 + (6 minus V)/2 = V/4
(12 minus V)/4 + (6 minus V)/2 + V/4 = 0
questions.concept: Writing each branch current as (far-end potential minus node potential)/R and keeping the in-equals-out sign convention consistent across every branch.
questions.why: Current into A from each source branch is (source voltage minus V)/R, and current out through the ground branch is V/4, so in equals out gives option c and V = 6.00 V. Option a flips the sign on the incoming branches only; option b drops the drops across the 4 and 2 ohm resistors; option d adds the outgoing current instead of subtracting it, so it mixes conventions and yields a negative node voltage.

questions.q: Two charges of 2.0 nC and minus 2.0 nC are 1.0 mm apart. What is the potential at a point 5.0 cm from the centre of the dipole, at 60 degrees to the dipole axis?
questions.concept: Forming p = q d first, then applying V = k p cos theta / r squared with the far-field condition r much greater than d checked.
questions.why: p = (2.0e-9)(1.0e-3) = 2.0e-12 C m, and r/d = 50 so the far-field form is valid. V = (8.99e9)(2.0e-12)(0.500)/(0.050 squared) = 3.6 V. 7.2 V drops the cos 60 factor, 6.2 V uses sin 60 in place of cos 60, and 0.18 V divides by r instead of r squared.

questions.q: At the same distance r from a dipole, how does the field on the axis compare with the field on the equatorial plane?
options: Half as large, and parallel to p.
Equal in magnitude, but perpendicular to p.
Four times as large, because the axial field falls as one over r cubed while the equatorial field falls as one over r to the fourth.
Twice as large and parallel to p, while the equatorial field is antiparallel to p.
questions.concept: The two standard far-field dipole results, 2kp over r cubed on the axis and kp over r cubed on the bisector, and their opposite directions.
questions.why: Both fields fall as one over r cubed, but the axial value is 2kp/r cubed and the equatorial value is kp/r cubed, a ratio of exactly 2. The axial field points along p, whereas on the bisector only the components running from the positive toward the negative charge survive, so that field is antiparallel to p.

questions.q: A dipole of moment 2.0e-12 C m sits at 30 degrees to a uniform field of 3.0e5 N/C. What is the torque on it?
options: Zero, because the net force on a dipole in a uniform field is zero.
questions.concept: Applying tau = p E sin theta with theta measured between p and E, and distinguishing zero net force from zero torque.
questions.why: tau = (2.0e-12)(3.0e5) sin 30 = (6.0e-7)(0.500) = 3.0e-7 N m. The 5.2e-7 value uses cos 30 instead of sin 30 (that is the size of the potential energy, not the torque), 6.0e-7 omits the angular factor altogether, and zero confuses vanishing net force with vanishing torque.

questions.q: A 177 pF air-spaced parallel-plate capacitor is charged to 100 V and then disconnected from the battery. A slab of dielectric constant 5.0 is slid fully between the plates. What is the new potential difference?
questions.concept: Identifying which quantity is held fixed: with the battery disconnected Q is constant, so V = Q/C falls by the factor kappa.
questions.why: Q = (177 pF)(100 V) = 17.7 nC is fixed once the battery is removed. C becomes 5.0 times 177 pF = 885 pF, so V = Q/C = 17.7 nC / 885 pF = 20 V, i.e. V-nought over kappa. 100 V would be right only if the battery had stayed connected, and 500 V has the factor of kappa inverted.

questions.q: Explain why a student who finds the node voltage of a network with the load still connected, and then uses that value as V_Th, gets the wrong load current — and why the error vanishes as the load resistance grows.
questions.concept: V_Th is the open-circuit voltage; loading the network before measuring it double-counts the load's effect.
questions.why: A full answer says that the node voltage measured with the load in place is already depressed by the current the load draws through the network's internal resistance. Feeding that depressed value into I = V_Th/(R_Th + R_L) applies the loading correction a second time, so the predicted current is too small. In the worked circuit the true V_Th is 8.0 V while the loaded node voltage is 6.0 V, giving 1.13 A instead of the correct 1.50 A. It should add that as R_L grows the load current tends to zero, the drop across R_Th tends to zero, and the loaded node voltage tends to the open-circuit value — which is why the mistake is invisible for very large loads and why the correct procedure is to delete the load before finding V_oc.

questions.q: Explain why dividing the emf by the external resistance alone always overestimates the current from a real cell, and why the size of that overestimate depends on the ratio r to R rather than on r by itself.
questions.concept: The role of r in the series total, and the fractional-error structure of the approximation I = emf/R.
questions.why: A full answer says the current is set by the total resistance of the loop, emf divided by (R + r), because the same current must pass through the internal resistance as through the load. Dropping r shrinks the denominator, so the estimate is always too big. Writing emf/(R + r) as (emf/R) times 1/(1 + r/R) shows the fractional error is governed by r/R, so a 0.5 ohm internal resistance is a 9 percent error against a 5 ohm load but only a 0.9 percent error against a 55 ohm load. It should conclude that r alone is not enough to judge whether the approximation is safe.

questions.q: Explain why the formula V = k p cos theta over r squared must not be used at distances comparable with the charge separation, and what has to be done instead.
questions.concept: The far-field (r much greater than d) approximation behind the dipole potential, and the exact two-charge superposition that replaces it.
questions.why: A full answer says the formula is not exact: it comes from V = kq/r_plus minus kq/r_minus after approximating the difference in the two distances by d cos theta, a step that assumes r is much greater than d. When r is comparable with d the two distances differ by a large fraction of themselves, the approximation collapses, and the formula can be badly wrong — for instance it wrongly predicts a finite potential on the axis at the location of a charge, where the true potential diverges. Instead one must add the exact point-charge potentials kq/r_plus and minus kq/r_minus using the actual geometric distances from each charge to the field point. It should note the practical test: check r/d, and that a ratio of order 10 or more makes the far-field form safe.

questions.q: Explain why the energy stored in an isolated charged capacitor falls when a dielectric slab is inserted, and where that energy goes.
questions.concept: Energy bookkeeping at constant charge, U = Q squared over 2C, and the mechanical work done by the fringing field on the slab.
questions.why: A full answer uses U = Q squared / 2C at fixed Q: inserting the slab multiplies C by kappa, so U falls by the factor kappa — from 8.85e-7 J to 1.77e-7 J for the worked numbers with kappa = 5. It then accounts for the missing energy mechanically: the non-uniform fringing field at the edge of the plates polarises the slab and pulls it inward, so the field does positive work on the slab as it enters. The stored electrical energy is converted into that work, appearing as kinetic energy of the slab and ultimately as heat when it is held in place. It should note that with the battery still connected the bookkeeping is different, because the battery then exchanges energy with the capacitor and the stored energy rises instead.

checks.topic: Week 4 Algorithm Concepts taken as practice: tracing the lecture's own algorithms by hand and writing them out. You trace the sum-and-count flowchart to a printed value and a decision count, work the maximum-of-a-set problem through the five development steps, and write the refined pseudocode using sequence, selection and repetition correctly. You then apply the Big O loop rules to concrete code fragments — a decrementing loop, a halving loop, nested loops — and diagnose faulty or wasteful solutions: a maximum initialised to zero, selection used where repetition was needed, and an O(n squared) pairwise comparison where one pass would do.

questions.q: Trace the lecture's flowchart: sum = 0; count = 0; then repeat { enter n; sum = sum + n; count = count + 1; is count < 5? if YES go back to 'enter n' }; print sum. The user enters 3, 1, 4, 1, 5. What is printed, and how many times is the decision box evaluated?
options: 14 is printed; the decision is evaluated 5 times.
14 is printed; the decision is evaluated 4 times.
9 is printed; the decision is evaluated 5 times.
15 is printed; the decision is evaluated 6 times.
questions.concept: Tracing a post-tested repetition loop: order of update and test, and counting decision evaluations
questions.why: The body runs once per number, so all five values are added: 3+1+4+1+5 = 14. The decision sits at the end of the body, so it is reached once per pass — five times, the fifth of which is false and exits.

questions.q: A student implements 'find the maximum' by setting max = 0 before the loop and then replacing max whenever an input exceeds it. On which input does this give a wrong answer?
options: A list of only negative numbers.
A list in which the maximum value appears more than once.
A list that is already sorted in descending order.
A list containing an odd number of elements.
questions.concept: Initialising the running maximum: why the seed must come from the data, not from a constant
questions.why: If every value is below zero, no input ever exceeds the seed, so the algorithm reports 0 — a value that is not in the list at all. Duplicates, sorted order and list length do not affect the comparison at all.

questions.q: A fragment runs two nested loops, each from 1 to n with the innermost statement executing once per pair, and afterwards a separate single loop from 1 to n. What is its time complexity?
options: O(n)
O(n squared)
O(n cubed)
O(n log n)
questions.concept: Applying the nested-loop rule (count the innermost statement's executions) and taking the dominant term
questions.why: The nested pair executes its innermost statement n times n, and the trailing loop adds n more; the faster-growing term governs the growth rate, so the fragment is quadratic. Two loops side by side do not multiply, and nothing here divides a loop variable.

questions.q: A team has already written 'Declare and initialize variables / Input numbers / Determine maximum number and output result'. They now rewrite the middle line as a loop that runs until a sentinel value is entered, prompting the user, accepting a number, comparing it with the maximum and incrementing a counter. Which development step are they performing?
options: Step 3: high-level algorithm development
Step 4: algorithm refinement
Step 2: problem analysis
Step 5: algorithm review
questions.concept: Recognising stepwise refinement: adding detail to an existing high-level step rather than producing or judging the algorithm
questions.why: The high-level algorithm already exists; expanding one of its lines into its constituent detail is exactly stepwise refinement. Step 3 produced the three lines, Step 2 settled the starting and ending points before any lines were written, and Step 5 asks whether the finished algorithm solves the problem.

questions.q: A student writes: sum = 0; count = 0; IF count < 5 THEN { enter n; sum = sum + n; count = count + 1 }; print sum. They intended to add five numbers but the program prints the first number entered. What is the fault?
options: The condition is tested before count has been initialised.
A selection construct is not permitted to contain assignment statements.
They used selection where repetition is needed, so the body executes at most once.
The counter is incremented after the addition instead of before it.
questions.concept: Selection versus repetition: a condition that guards a block once versus a condition that returns control to the same block
questions.why: IF tests its condition once and then falls through, so exactly one number is read; only a repetition construct sends control back to the same steps while the condition holds. count is initialised on the line above, selection may contain assignments, and the order of the two updates within the body is immaterial here.

questions.q: What is the time complexity of: i = n; while i > 1 do i = i / 2?
options: O(n)
O(log n)
questions.concept: The loop rule for a variable divided by a constant amount
questions.why: The loop variable is divided by a constant each pass, which is the stated condition for O(log n): each pass removes a fixed fraction, so the number of passes counts the halvings rather than the values. Halving does not merely remove half the work once, which is what the O(n/2) answer assumes, and the loop clearly depends on n so it is not constant.

questions.q: Which of these is a properly formed high-level algorithm (Step 3) for the meeting-scheduling task?
options: A single instruction: 'Schedule the meeting at a time that suits everybody.'
A version that names the exact calendar API calls, the request format and the data structures used to read each attendee's availability before any overall shape is settled.
A version that identifies the attendees and finds the common free slots, and stops there because the remaining steps are details.
Identify attendees; find common free slots; choose one and tell everyone; get confirmation; if negative iterate from the slot-finding step, else identify the location.
questions.concept: What 'high-level' means in Step 3: the main parts of the whole solution, with minor detail deferred but nothing essential missing
questions.why: A high-level algorithm covers the main parts of the complete solution and omits only minor detail, which is what the fourth option does end to end. Restating the goal is not an algorithm, specifying API calls is refinement done far too early, and stopping halfway leaves the solution incomplete rather than merely undetailed.

questions.q: To find the maximum of n numbers, a student compares every number with every other number using two nested loops and reports the number that was never beaten. On the test data it gives the correct answer. What is the objection to this solution?
options: It is incorrect whenever two or more numbers tie for the maximum, because then no number is strictly never beaten.
It uses selection where repetition is required by the problem.
It violates the finiteness characteristic, because two nested loops never terminate.
It is O(n squared) where a single pass keeping a running maximum is O(n).
questions.concept: Step 5 review: reducing complexity when a correct algorithm does asymptotically more work than necessary
questions.why: Correctness is not the only bar; Step 5 explicitly asks whether the complexity can be reduced, and comparing all pairs does quadratic work for a result obtainable in one linear pass. The tie objection fails if the comparison is non-strict, the solution uses repetition throughout, and nested loops with fixed bounds do terminate.

questions.q: Explain why seeding the running maximum with the first input, rather than with 0, fixes the negative-numbers bug — trace a short input to show the mechanism.
questions.concept: Correct initialisation of an accumulator that must be drawn from the data set
questions.why: A full answer states the mechanism: the running maximum is meant to hold the largest value seen so far, so before any value has been seen it has no legitimate contents; seeding it with 0 silently inserts a value that is not in the list and that the comparison can never remove if every real value is smaller. Seeding it with the first input makes the invariant true from the start — after k inputs, max is the largest of those k. A trace should be shown: for the list -7, -3, -9 with max = 0, no comparison ever succeeds and the answer is 0, which is not in the list; with max = -7, the second input replaces it with -3, the third does not, and -3 is reported, which is correct. The same argument explains why the loop must then compare from the second input onwards.

questions.q: Explain why the refined maximum-of-a-set algorithm needs a sentinel value, and say exactly what breaks in the loop if the sentinel is removed and nothing replaces it.
questions.concept: Loop termination conditions: a repetition construct needs something that makes its condition eventually false
questions.why: A full answer explains that the problem statement does not fix how many numbers the user will enter, so the algorithm cannot use a fixed count; the sentinel is the agreed value whose entry makes the loop condition false, and it is what turns an open-ended input into a terminating repetition. Remove it with no replacement and the condition never becomes false: the loop prompts forever, the counter keeps growing, and the steps after the loop — identify the maximum and output the result — are never reached, so the algorithm produces no output at all. This also breaks the finiteness characteristic, which requires a limited and countable number of executed instructions. The legitimate alternative is to ask for the count of numbers first and loop that many times.

questions.q: Explain why replacing a nested-loop solution with a single-pass solution changes the algorithm's behaviour on large inputs, when both give identical output on small test data.
questions.concept: Growth rate versus measured result: why correctness on test data cannot reveal an efficiency fault
questions.why: A full answer separates output from cost. Both algorithms compute the same function, so no comparison of results will ever distinguish them; what differs is the number of times the innermost statement executes, which is roughly n times n for the nested version and roughly n for the single pass. On small test data the two counts are close enough that the difference is invisible, which is precisely why the fault survives testing. As n grows the ratio between them grows with n as well, so the gap widens without limit: ten times more data costs the single pass ten times more work and the nested version a hundred times more. The answer should conclude that this is why Step 5 asks whether complexity can be reduced, and why priori analysis of growth rate is needed rather than a timing run on a small case.

questions.q: Explain why the sum-and-count flowchart puts its decision at the end of the loop body rather than at the beginning, and what would change in the trace if the test were moved to the top.
questions.concept: Placement of the loop test: post-tested versus pre-tested repetition, and its effect on the number of executions
questions.why: A full answer explains that with the test at the end, the body is guaranteed to execute at least once before any condition is examined, which suits this algorithm because count is 0 at entry and the first number must be read unconditionally. The test then acts as a continue-or-exit decision after each addition, and with the target of five numbers it is evaluated five times, failing on the fifth. Moving the test to the top makes it a pre-tested loop of the 'while condition is true, do' form: the condition is examined before the first number is read, so it is evaluated six times for the same five additions, and if the initial state ever failed the condition the body would not execute at all. The answer should note that both arrangements can be made to sum five numbers, but the initial values and the number of condition evaluations must be adjusted to match.

recapCandidates.topic: The limit of f at c and the value f(c) are two independent readings taken from the same graph, and continuity is the separate claim that they agree. Everything in this week follows from that split: the limit is built only from x ≠ c, so redefining f(c) can repair a hole but can never repair a jump or an asymptote.
recapCandidates.whyMisunderstood: Students hold the model 'the limit is what you get by plugging c in', and it survives because on every unbroken graph they meet — lines, polynomials, |x| — substitution does give the right answer, so the model is only ever punished at a hole, a jump, or a 0/0.
whyQuestions: Why does the definition of continuity list three conditions instead of simply saying lim(x→c) f(x) = f(c)?
Why is f(c) read from the shaded dot on a graph and never from an open circle, even when the open circle is the height both branches approach?
Why can direct substitution be trusted for lim(x→3) (2x + 1) but not for lim(x→1) (x² − 1)/(x − 1)?
Why can a removable discontinuity be repaired by redefining the function at a single point while a jump discontinuity cannot be repaired at all?
Why does lim(x→3⁺) f(x) = +∞ count as the limit failing to exist, when we have written down an answer for it?
recapCandidates.goodAnswerContains:
It says that lim(x→c) f(x) is computed from values of f at points other than c, so f(c) can be changed, removed or misplaced without altering the limit — which is exactly why the equality of limit and value has to be imposed as its own condition rather than derived.
It matches each type of discontinuity to the condition it breaks: removable breaks (i) or (iii) with the limit intact, so setting f(c) := L repairs it; jump and infinite break (ii) itself, because L⁻ ≠ L⁺ or a side runs to ±∞, and (ii) is a fact about the branches that no single value can touch.
It carries a concrete instance through: (x²−1)/(x−1) has limit 2 at x = 1 with f(1) undefined, so a hole at (1, 2) that redefinition fills — set against a graph whose branches arrive at 3 and −4, where the limit is DNE and no value of f(2) helps.
recapCandidates.workedExample: Take f(x) = (x² − 1)/(x − 1) at x = 1. Step 1: substitute — (1 − 1)/(1 − 1) = 0/0, indeterminate, so substitution decides nothing; it only tells us numerator and denominator share the factor (x − 1). Step 2: factor the numerator as a difference of two squares, x² − 1 = (x − 1)(x + 1). Step 3: cancel, legally, because a limit as x → 1 only uses x ≠ 1, so x − 1 ≠ 0 throughout: f(x) = x + 1 for all x ≠ 1. Step 4: one-sided limits — lim(x→1⁻)(x + 1) = 2 and lim(x→1⁺)(x + 1) = 2; they agree on a finite number, so lim(x→1) f(x) = 2. Step 5: the value — f(1) is still 0/0, undefined, because cancelling changed the formula but never the domain. Step 6: classify — limit exists and is finite, value missing, so a removable discontinuity: the line y = x + 1 with an open circle at (1, 2). Step 7: repair — define F(x) = f(x) for x ≠ 1 and F(1) = 2; now F(1) is defined, the limit exists, and they are equal, so F is continuous at 1. Step 8: the contrast that makes the point — on a graph whose left branch runs into 3 at x = 2 and whose right branch starts from −4, with a shaded dot at (2, 1), we get lim(x→2⁻) = 3, lim(x→2⁺) = −4, so lim(x→2) f(x) = DNE and f(2) = 1. Here step 7 is impossible: 3 ≠ −4 is a statement about the branches, and every candidate value for f(2) leaves it standing.

recapCandidates.topic: Big O does not tell you how long an algorithm takes; it describes the growth rate — how the work changes as the input size n changes. That is why the algorithm with the enormous constant, 1000N, is the better one even though it is a thousand times slower than N squared at N = 1, and why the two only trade places at N = 1000.
recapCandidates.whyMisunderstood: Students treat a Big O class as a speed label stuck to the algorithm — 'O(n squared) is slow, O(n) is fast' — and the model survives because textbook and exam examples always use inputs large enough that the lower-growth algorithm really is the faster one, so the wrong reasoning keeps producing the right answer.
whyQuestions: Why does Big O describe a growth rate rather than a number of seconds?
Why is 1000N considered the more efficient algorithm when its constant is a thousand times larger than the constant in N squared?
Why does the comparison between 1000N and N squared flip exactly at N = 1000, and what does that tell you about which algorithm to choose for small inputs?
Why can two algorithms that are both O(n) still differ by a factor of ten in the time they actually take?
Why does the course still need posterior analysis at all, once priori analysis has told us the growth rates of every candidate?
recapCandidates.goodAnswerContains:
A real explanation says what Big O is a statement about: the number of times the work is done as a function of n, counted from the structure of the algorithm before any code exists, not a measured duration.
It shows the crossover concretely — 1000N beats N squared only once N passes 1000 — and draws the right conclusion: growth rate decides which algorithm wins eventually, and 'eventually' can be a long way off.
It closes the loop by naming the two analyses: priori analysis gives the growth rate and is machine- and language-independent; posterior analysis, after implementation, is the only thing that gives actual space and running time.
recapCandidates.workedExample:
Compare two algorithms for the same problem: A does 1000N steps, B does N squared steps.
N = 1:      A = 1,000        B = 1              -> B wins by 1000x
N = 10:     A = 10,000       B = 100            -> B wins by 100x
N = 100:    A = 100,000      B = 10,000         -> B still wins by 10x
N = 1000:   A = 1,000,000    B = 1,000,000      -> they tie; this is the crossover
N = 10,000: A = 10,000,000   B = 100,000,000    -> A wins by 10x
N = 100,000:A = 100,000,000  B = 10,000,000,000 -> A wins by 100x

Read off the mechanism: multiplying N by 10 multiplies A's work by 10 and B's work by 100. A's cost grows in step with the data; B's grows with the square of it, so every tenfold increase in data costs B a further factor of ten relative to A. Nothing about the constant 1000 can stop that, because the constant is applied once while the extra factor of N compounds — which is exactly what Big O keeps and the constant is exactly what it discards, leaving O(N) for A and O(N squared) for B.

The honest caveat, which is the part students miss: if this system will only ever see N below 1000, B is the right choice and Big O is not the deciding argument. Big O tells you which algorithm survives growth; it is posterior analysis, after implementation, that tells you how many seconds either one takes on your machine today.
